data.text/html:
PrefixSpan: mining sequential patterns by growing prefixes

An interactive companion to Philippe Fournier-Viger's video "The PrefixSpan algorithm".
Customers buy things over time: first apple and bread, then cake, then apple again. Which sub-sequences of purchases show up for many customers?
PrefixSpan answers that by growing patterns one item at a time, depth-first, and by only ever looking at a shrinking projected database, so it never wastes time on patterns that don't exist in the data. Every section below has something to step through, click or slide.

data.text/markdown:
1 · Sequences, itemsets, support

A sequence database is a list of sequences. Each sequence is an ordered list of itemsets; items inside one itemset happen at the same time (bought together), and itemsets later in the sequence happen after. The video writes a sequence like ⟨(a,b),(c),(a)⟩: apple and bread together, then cake, then apple. We write it compactly as (a,b)(c)(a). Two ways a pattern can grow, and the video stresses not to confuse them:
notation meaning name
(a,b) a and b together in the same itemset itemset-extension (the video's "_b")
(a)(b) a, and later b sequence-extension
A pattern is contained in a sequence if its itemsets can be matched, in order, to itemsets of the sequence that are supersets of them. The support of a pattern is the number of sequences that contain it. With minsup = 3, we want every pattern contained in ≥ 3 sequences. Why PrefixSpan? Earlier algorithms such as GSP generate candidate patterns by joining smaller patterns without looking at the data, so they may waste time counting patterns that appear nowhere. PrefixSpan only extends a pattern with items it actually sees in the (projected) database.

data.text/markdown:
2 · The algorithm

The video's simple version, as recursive pseudocode: 
PrefixSpan(prefix s, projected DB D|s, minsup):
    scan D|s once → support of every item that can extend s
    for each item x with support ≥ minsup:
        output s' = s extended by x
        build projected DB D|s'      # keep only what comes *after* the first match
        PrefixSpan(s', D|s', minsup)
Projection. For a prefix, each sequence keeps only the part after the first occurrence of the prefix; sequences that don't contain the prefix are dropped. If the match ended in the middle of an itemset, the rest of that itemset stays as a partial itemset, written (_b). Counting extensions of a prefix whose last itemset is L:
  • itemset-extension x (x sorts after L's items): x appears in the partial itemset (_x), or in a later itemset that contains all of L plus x.
  • sequence-extension x: x appears in any later, complete itemset.
The implementation below works with pointers (sequence, itemset, item) into the original database (the pseudo-projection of Section 4), and records a full trace of the depth-first search.

data.text/markdown:
3 · Watch the depth-first search

Step through PrefixSpan on the video's database. Left: the search tree, exactly like the video's picture: the empty sequence at the root, each child is the prefix extended by one item. Green nodes are frequent and get extended further; grey ✕ nodes are counted once in the projected database and then pruned: nothing that starts with them can be frequent. The orange node is where the algorithm is right now. Right: that node's projected database (struck-out grey = removed by projection, _ marks a partial itemset) and the count table from a single scan, split into itemset-extensions (together, (…,x)) and sequence-extensions (later, (…)(x)).

4 · Optimization 1: pseudo-projection (pointers instead of copies)

Copying the database for every prefix costs a lot of time and memory: there may be thousands of prefixes. The video's fix: don't copy, point. A projected database is just one pointer per sequence into the original database, marking where the prefix's first match ended. Build a prefix yourself by clicking. Buttons show the support each extension would have (green if ≥ minsup). Watch the blue pointers slide right through the original sequences, consumed items turn grey, and sequences without a match fade out. The toggle applies the video's second optimization: remove infrequent items (like d) from the database once, after the first scan, so every later scan is shorter.

5 · What makes PrefixSpan slow? Lower the minimum support

The video lists what drives the cost: minsup first (lower it and the time can grow exponentially), then the database: number of sequences, their length, how similar they are, and the number of distinct items. Generate a random sequence database below (seeded, so it's reproducible). Item popularity follows a skewed (Zipf-like) law so some items are common, like real shopping data. The chart sweeps minsup from 60 % of the sequences down to your chosen floor. Runs are capped at 20 000 patterns so the notebook stays responsive.
Sample of the generated database: (b,f)(a)(b)(c)(c,f,l)(a) · (b)(b,d) · (d)(b) · (a) · (b,c)(b)(a)(b,l)(c,d)(a,b)(b) …

6 · Sandbox: mine your own sequences

One sequence per line. Write itemsets in parentheses, (ab)(c)(a) or (a,b)(c)(a), or separate itemsets with spaces, ab c a. Single letters are items; use commas for longer item names, e.g. (milk,bread)(eggs). The video notes PrefixSpan is easy to extend with constraints; here you can cap the pattern length (number of items), a one-line check in the recursion.

Recap

idea what to remember where you played with it
sequence DB & support ordered itemsets; support = # sequences containing the pattern §1 table
itemset- vs sequence-extension (a,b) together ≠ (a)(b) later; counted separately ("_b") §3 count tables, §4 buttons
database projection keep only what follows the first match of the prefix; drop non-matching sequences §3 right panel
depth-first search extend one frequent prefix all the way down, then backtrack §3 search tree
pruning (anti-monotonicity) an infrequent prefix can't have frequent extensions (d, (a)(b), …) §3 grey ✕ nodes
only real patterns candidates come from the data, never from blind joins (vs GSP) §5 right chart
pseudo-projection one pointer per sequence instead of a copy, ~10× less memory §4
remove infrequent items drop d once after the first scan; every later scan is shorter §4 toggle
performance minsup ↓ ⇒ patterns & time ↑ (exponentially); DB size, length, #items matter §5 sliders
constraints easy to add, e.g. max length, max gap §6
Source: Philippe Fournier-Viger, “The PrefixSpan algorithm” (video). A fast Java implementation is in the open-source SPMF library.
